feedback: If a learner thinks the bee is deliberately helping, highlight that it came for food (nectar, and some pollen to eat) yet still left flour/pollen on the next flower — the pollination happens by accident.
If a learner stops at 'pollen moved', prompt them to say what the pollen then allows the flower to do (make seeds, then fruit).
activities.intendedInsight: Pollen transfer is accidental — it sticks to and rubs off a fuzzy visitor — and it is a separate, earlier step from seed formation and fruit growth.
learnerActions: Sprinkle flour (standing for pollen) on the centre of a first paper 'flower', then let a pipe-cleaner or cotton-wool 'bee' visit it so flour clings to the fuzzy 'bee'.
Touch the 'bee' to a second paper 'flower' and look at the flour (pollen) left behind.
Describe how the pollen got from the first flower to the second without the bee meaning to pollinate the flower.
Discuss which part of this is pollination (the pollen moving between flowers), and what comes after it (seeds, then fruit).
activities.title: Hands-on pollen transfer with a flour-dusted 'bee'

feedback: If a learner orders fruit before pollen transfer, point back to the idea that fruit forms after pollen reaches a flower's stigma (in this story, carried from the previous flower by the bee).

If a learner treats pollination as pollen staying within one flower, remind them that when bees pollinate, they usually carry pollen to a different flower (some plants can pollinate themselves, but bees are the movers in this story).
If a learner names only bees, note that butterflies, hoverflies and beetles also pollinate, and that a single crop may be visited by more than one kind.
If a learner says 'nothing would happen' with no pollinators, revisit the no-bees comparison showing flowers that never set fruit.
activities.intendedInsight: Pollination is a sequence that leads to seeds and fruit, carried out by several kinds of insect, and losing pollinators would reduce the fruit and vegetables we grow.
learnerActions: Put the pollination steps in order: bee visits flower for nectar → pollen sticks to bee → bee visits next flower → pollen rubs off → flower makes seeds → fruit grows.

Look at several pollinators (bees, butterflies, hoverflies, beetles) and work out which insects can visit a given crop, noticing that the SAME crop is often visited by more than one kind — bees are not the only ones, so there is no single exclusive partner.
Answer: what would happen to a garden or orchard if the pollinating insects vanished, and why?
activities.title: Order the steps and explore pollinator variety

feedback: If the account has the bee deliberately helping, remind them the bee is looking for food (mainly nectar, plus some pollen to eat) and pollinates the flower by accident.
If the account conflates honey-making with pollination, separate them: honey is made from nectar in the hive; pollination is the pollen moving between flowers.
activities.intendedInsight: Narrating the bee's visit from its own point of view consolidates both the accidental mechanism and the mutual benefit.
learnerActions: Take the role of a bee and tell or write a short account of visiting flowers: why you go (nectar), what sticks to you, and what you leave behind at the next flower.
Explain 'the deal' between the bee and the plant — what each one gets.
Finish by saying what would happen to the plants, and to our food, if bees like you stopped visiting.
activities.title: A day in the life of a bee: tell the story
